pos: n. (a raised brasen platform set in the temple court)
etymology: From the Old French escadafault, a raised stage. The word occurs once, of the brass platform Solomon built for the dedication of the temple — a place to stand that he used to kneel.
biblical_def: The Chronicler records a detail Kings omits: “For Solomon had made a brasen scaffold, of five cubits long, and five cubits broad, and three cubits high, and had set it in the midst of the court: and upon it he stood, and kneeled down upon his knees before all the congregation of Israel, and spread forth his hands toward heaven” (2 Chronicles 6:13). The platform was built to make the king visible, and the first thing he did on it was go down on his knees in front of the nation. The prayer he offered from that posture anticipates the exile: “If they sin against thee, (for there is no man which sinneth not,) and thou be angry with them, and deliver them over before their enemies, and they carry them away captives unto a land far off or near” (2 Chronicles 6:36). And it asks that God would hear from heaven rather than from the house just built: “Then hear thou from the heavens, even from thy dwelling place, their prayer and their supplications, and maintain their cause, and forgive thy people which have sinned against thee” (2 Chronicles 6:39). God's answer came that night with a condition attached: “If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scaffold as a temporary gallery or stage raised either for shows or spectators; an elevated platform.
webster_full: SCAFFOLD, n. A temporary gallery or stage raised either for shows or spectators.
SCAFFOLD, n. A stage or elevated platform for the execution of a criminal.
BRASEN, a. Made of brass; pertaining to brass; in Scripture, of the altar, laver and pillars of the temple.
DEDICATE, v.t. To set apart and consecrate to a divine Being, or to a sacred purpose.
SUPPLICATION, n. Entreaty; humble and earnest prayer in worship.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 6:13

For Solomon had made a brasen scaffold, of five cubits long, and five cubits broad, and three cubits high, and had set it in the midst of the court: and upon it he stood, and kneeled down upon his knees before all the congregation of Israel, and spread forth his hands toward heaven,
2 Chronicles 6:36

If they sin against thee, (for there is no man which sinneth not,) and thou be angry with them, and deliver them over before their enemies, and they carry them away captives unto a land far off or near;
2 Chronicles 6:39
Then hear thou from the heavens, even from thy dwelling place, their prayer and their supplications, and maintain their cause, and forgive thy people which have sinned against thee.
2 Chronicles 7:14

If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
corruption_summary: 2 Chronicles 7:14 is lifted out of the dedication prayer and applied to nations that were never in covenant with God, turning a promise to Israel into a political programme.
corruption_paragraphs: No verse in Chronicles is more often detached from its setting. If my people, which are called by my name is God's direct answer to the prayer Solomon offered from the brasen scaffold, concerning the covenant nation, the temple just dedicated, and the land promised to Abraham. It is regularly recited over modern nations as a formula for national revival, as though any country stood where Israel stood. No nation since has been in that covenant. The application that Scripture does authorise runs through the church, which is now the people called by His name, and it runs through repentance rather than through politics.

What the passage does teach, and teaches with force, is the order of God's dealing: humble themselves, pray, seek His face, turn from their wicked ways — and only then, hear, forgive, heal. Solomon's own prayer had assumed the same order and had assumed the sin, parenthetically and without argument: for there is no man which sinneth not. A king built a platform so the nation could see him, climbed it, and knelt. That is the posture from which the promise was given, and any use of the verse that skips the kneeling has taken the answer without the prayer.
roots_summary: Hebrew kiyyor (H3595), a basin or platform; nechosheth (H5178), brass; barak (H1288), to kneel; kana (H3665), to humble oneself.
roots_lines: Hebrew kiyyor (H3595) — a laver or round platform; the brasen scaffold of 2 Chronicles 6:13.
Hebrew nechosheth (H5178) — brass, copper; the metal of the temple court furnishings.
Hebrew barak (H1288) — to kneel, bless; he kneeled down upon his knees.
Hebrew kana (H3665) — to humble, bring low; shall humble themselves, 2 Chronicles 7:14.
Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn, return; turn from their wicked ways.

“For there is no man which sinneth not” — assumed in the dedication prayer.
“If my people, which are called by my name” — the answer, with its order intact.

pos: v. (racked; put to extreme torment, with deliverance offered and refused)
etymology: From the Latin torquere, to twist. The Greek word in Hebrews names the tympanum, a rack or frame on which a man was stretched and beaten. It occurs once, in the roll of faith.
biblical_def: The eleventh of Hebrews turns, midway, from triumphs to torments, and the hinge is this verse: “Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection” (Hebrews 11:35). The clause that carries the weight is not accepting deliverance. Release was offered and declined, because accepting it meant denying the God who would raise them. The catalogue continues without softening: “And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Hebrews 11:36). The writer's verdict on these people is the most startling sentence in the chapter: “(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Hebrews 11:38). And then he says that none of them received the promise in their lifetime: “And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise” (Hebrews 11:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines torture as extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; and to torture as to pain to extremity, to torment.
webster_full: TORTURE, n. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; pang; agony; torment.
TORTURE, v.t. To pain to extremity; to torment; to punish with torture, as by the rack.
MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the truth, particularly of the Christian faith.
RACK, n. An engine of torture, on which the limbs of a criminal were stretched.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint; rescue from danger.
scriptures: Hebrews 11:35
Women received their dead raised to life again : and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection:
Hebrews 11:36
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
Hebrews 11:38
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Hebrews 11:39
And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise:
corruption_summary: Faith is redefined as the means of obtaining deliverance, which requires the second half of Hebrews 11 to be quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 11 is preached as far as verse 35a and rarely further. Faith that stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, and turned to flight the armies of the aliens makes an encouraging sermon. The same sentence continues into men who were sawn asunder and women who refused release under torture, and the writer applies the word faith to both halves without any change of tone. Any doctrine that identifies faith with escape from suffering has to cut this chapter in two, and the chapter is not divisible: the identical faith produced deliverance in some and endurance under torture in others, and God commended both.

The reason given is the doctrine that holds the whole chapter together — that they might obtain a better resurrection. These people refused a real offer of release because they were reckoning on something further out than release. The writer says plainly that none of them received the promise in their lifetimes, and that God provided some better thing so that they should not be made perfect apart from us. That is the Reformed account of the Christian's hope: not a guarantee about circumstances in this life, but a certainty about the resurrection that makes present loss a bearable exchange. Of whom the world was not worthy is God's estimate of people the world had finished with.
roots_summary: Greek tumpanizo (G5178), to beat on a rack or frame; apolutrosis (G629), release, deliverance; kreitton (G2909), better; anastasis (G386), resurrection.
roots_lines: Greek tumpanizo (G5178) — to stretch and beat on the tympanum; only Hebrews 11:35.
Greek apolutrosis (G629) — a release on payment; here the deliverance not accepted.
Greek kreitton (G2909) — better; a better resurrection, a better thing provided for us.
Greek anastasis (G386) — resurrection, a rising again.
Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness; having obtained a good report.
usage: “Others were tortured, not accepting deliverance” — release offered and refused.
“Of whom the world was not worthy” — the writer's estimate.
“Received not the promise” — none of them saw it in their lifetime.

pos: v. (drawn or carved in likeness upon a wall)
etymology: An older spelling of portrayed, from the Old French pourtraire, to draw forth. Both occurrences are in Ezekiel, and both describe images on a wall that drew Israel into idolatry.
biblical_def: Ezekiel is brought in vision to a hidden chamber in the temple and told to dig through the wall: “So I went in and saw; and behold every form of creeping things, and abominable beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel, pourtrayed upon the wall round about” (Ezekiel 8:10). Seventy elders stood in that room with censers in their hands, and the LORD gives their reasoning: “Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth” (Ezekiel 8:12). The second use makes wall-images the occasion of a national infatuation: “And that she increased her whoredoms: for when she saw men pourtrayed upon the wall, the images of the Chaldeans pourtrayed with vermilion” (Ezekiel 23:14). She sends for the men whose pictures she has seen. Against all of it stands the commandment in its own words: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth” (Exodus 20:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines portray as to paint or draw the likeness of anything in colors; to adorn with pictures.
webster_full: PORTRAY, v.t. To paint or draw the likeness of anything in colors; to describe in words.
PORTRAYED, pp. Drawn in colors; painted; described; adorned with pictures.
IMAGERY, n. Sensible representations, pictures, statues; forms of the fancy; the chambers of imagery.
VERMILION, n. A bright beautiful red color; a red pigment used in painting.
ABOMINATION, n. That which is abominable; hatred; detestation; in Scripture, an idol or idolatrous practice.
scriptures: Ezekiel 8:10
So I went in and saw; and behold every form of creeping things, and abominable beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel, pourtrayed upon the wall round about.
Ezekiel 8:12

Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth.
Ezekiel 23:14
And that she increased her whoredoms: for when she saw men pourtrayed upon the wall, the images of the Chaldeans pourtrayed with vermilion,
Exodus 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as something done in public at a shrine, while Ezekiel locates it in a private chamber whose owner is sure no one is watching.
corruption_paragraphs: The chambers of imagery are the most searching passage in Scripture on hidden sin. The seventy elders were not apostates in the street; they were the leadership of Israel, in the dark, each man in his own room, surrounded by pictures he had chosen, reasoning that the LORD seeth us not. The room was inside the temple. Ezekiel had to dig through a wall to find the door. Every element of the account is aimed at the respectable man whose visible life is orderly and whose private chamber is furnished with what he would not defend aloud.

The modern application is unavoidable and should be made plainly. Images pourtrayed upon a wall, viewed privately, believed to be unobserved, and productive of a desire that then seeks its object — Ezekiel 23 describes the sequence exactly, and the screen has made the chamber portable. Scripture's remedy is not primarily better concealment or stronger resolve but the truth the elders had denied: God sees. Our Lord located adultery in the look before it reaches the act, and the second commandment forbids the image before it forbids the bowing. Where the chamber of imagery is admitted and repented of, it is forgiven; where it is defended as private, Ezekiel says it is idolatry in the house of God.

“The LORD seeth us not” — the reasoning of the elders in the dark.
“When she saw men pourtrayed upon the wall” — the image that produced the desire.

pos: v. (to be distinguished from; to be made unlike another)
etymology: From the Latin differre, to carry apart. The word stands once in a question of three clauses that Paul aims at Corinthian pride, and it has been a text of the doctrine of grace ever since.
biblical_def: Paul asks three questions in one breath, and each closes a door: “For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). The first question asks the origin of any distinction between one man and another; the second denies that anything is held except by gift; the third exposes boasting as a claim to have originated what was given. He had already stated the purpose of God's choosing in the same letter: “But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1 Corinthians 1:27), with the reason attached: “That no flesh should glory in his presence” (1 Corinthians 1:29). And the only boasting left open is named: “But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). Everything a believer has, he received; and what is received cannot be boasted in.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines differ as to be unlike or distinct; to have qualities not the same; to vary.
webster_full: DIFFER, v.i. To be unlike or distinct in nature, qualities or form; to be various or different.
DIFFERENCE, n. The state of being unlike or distinct; distinction; disagreement.
GLORY, v.i. To boast; to be proud of; to exult with joy; to rejoice.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God; the divine influence renewing the heart.
MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 4:7
For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
1 Corinthians 1:27
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
1 Corinthians 1:29
That no flesh should glory in his presence .
1 Corinthians 1:30
But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption:
corruption_summary: The question is answered with something in the believer — a better decision, a greater openness, a more sincere heart — which is precisely the answer the verse forecloses.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 4:7 is the sharpest single-verse case against every doctrine that grounds salvation in the sinner. Asked who maketh thee to differ?, the synergist must ultimately answer: I did, at least at the decisive point. He may say it modestly — God offered and I accepted, God enabled and I cooperated, grace was available to all and I did not resist — but the difference between the saved man and his neighbour is finally traced to something in him that was not in the other. Paul's second question then falls: what hast thou that thou didst not receive? Augustine used this verse against Pelagius, and the argument has not been answered since.

The doctrine is not an abstraction but a cure for a particular disease, which is why Paul is writing it to Corinth. That church was dividing over teachers, ranking gifts, and priding itself on wisdom. The remedy applied is not better manners but a fact: nothing you hold is yours by origin. If election is unconditional, if the call is effectual, if faith itself is the gift of God and not of works, then boasting is excluded not by prohibition but by arithmetic. The same doctrine that humbles pride also destroys despair, since a salvation that never rested on the believer's contribution cannot be forfeited by his weakness.
roots_summary: Greek diakrino (G1252), to distinguish, make to differ; lambano (G2983), to receive; kauchaomai (G2744), to boast or glory; eklegomai (G1586), to choose out.
roots_lines: Greek diakrino (G1252) — to separate, distinguish; who maketh thee to differ.
Greek lambano (G2983) — to receive, take; what hast thou that thou didst not receive.
Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to boast, glory; why dost thou glory.
Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out, elect; God hath chosen the foolish things.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace, unmerited favour; the ground of every difference.

“What hast thou that thou didst not receive?” — and bolts it.
“That no flesh should glory in his presence” — the stated purpose of God's choosing.

pos: v. (to loose; to unfasten; to reverse what has been done)
etymology: From un- + do, Saxon undon, to unfasten. Scripture uses it twice, once of the burdens men are to loose from others, and once of what God will do to those who afflict His people.
biblical_def: Isaiah's great chapter on fasting defines the fast God chose in terms of what is loosed: “Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?” (Isaiah 58:6). The people had complained that God took no notice of their fasting, and He answers by describing a fast with no food in it at all. What follows is equally concrete: “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?” (Isaiah 58:7). Zephaniah gives the word to God as His own action: “Behold, at that time I will undo all that afflict thee: and I will save her that halteth, and gather her that was driven out; and I will get them praise and fame in every land where they have been put to shame” (Zephaniah 3:19). And the promise attached to Isaiah's fast is light: “Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the LORD shall be thy rereward” (Isaiah 58:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines undo as to reverse what has been done; to annul; to loose; to open what is shut or fastened.
webster_full: UNDO, v.t. To reverse what has been done; to annul; to bring to naught.
UNDO, v.t. To loose; to open; to take to pieces; to unfasten; to unravel.
FAST, n. Abstinence from food, voluntarily, as a religious mortification or humiliation.
OPPRESS, v.t. To load or burden with unreasonable impositions; to treat with unjust severity or hardship.
YOKE, n. A piece of timber fitted to the necks of oxen; a mark of servitude; slavery; bondage.
scriptures: Isaiah 58:6
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
Isaiah 58:7

Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?
Zephaniah 3:19

Behold, at that time I will undo all that afflict thee: and I will save her that halteth, and gather her that was driven out; and I will get them praise and fame in every land where they have been put to shame.
Isaiah 58:8
Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the LORD shall be thy rereward.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 58 is claimed as a mandate for a social gospel detached from doctrine, or else neutralised into a chapter about personal devotional habits.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 58 is fought over from both sides and rarely read as it stands. One party takes it as proof that God cares about justice and not about doctrine or worship, and builds a gospel of activism on it. But the chapter opens with God telling the prophet to cry aloud and shew His people their transgression, and it closes by commanding Sabbath-keeping and calling it a delight; it is a rebuke to false worship, not a replacement for worship. The people fasting in verse 3 were religiously observant and were smiting with the fist of wickedness on the same day.

The opposite party quietly reduces the chapter to interior piety — fast with the right attitude — and skips the list. The list will not be skipped. Loose the bands, undo the heavy burdens, let the oppressed go free, break every yoke, deal thy bread to the hungry, bring the poor that are cast out to thy house, cover the naked, hide not thyself from thine own flesh. These are the biblical categories, and they are personal and costly rather than abstract and political. The Reformed tradition has always held that faith without works is dead and that works are never the ground of acceptance. Isaiah 58 assumes both and treats them as a single obedience.

pos: n. pl. (those who drink; habitual takers of wine)
etymology: From drink, Saxon drincan. Joel addresses the word to a class of men and tells them to weep, because the locusts have taken away the thing their lives were organised around.
biblical_def: The prophet's first summons in the locust plague is to the men least likely to notice a national calamity: “Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth” (Joel 1:5). God reaches them through the loss of the very thing they loved; the supply fails, and the stupor breaks. The devastation is total and is described as an invading army: “For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion” (Joel 1:6). The purpose of the whole visitation is stated when the call to repentance comes: “Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12). And the promise on the far side is the restoration of exactly what was eaten: “And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you” (Joel 2:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines drinker as one who drinks; chiefly, one who drinks spirituous liquors to excess; a drunkard.
webster_full: DRINKER, n. One who drinks; chiefly, one who drinks spirituous liquors to excess; a drunkard; a tippler.
DRUNKARD, n. One given to ebriety or an excessive use of strong liquor; a person who habitually is drunk.
WINE, n. The fermented juice of grapes; in Scripture, both a blessing that cheereth God and man, and a mocker.
SOBRIETY, n. Habitual soberness or temperance; freedom from intoxication.
LOCUST, n. An insect which multiplies to an immense degree and devastates whole countries.
scriptures: Joel 1:5
Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth.
Joel 1:6
For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion.
Joel 2:12
Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning:
Joel 2:25
And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
corruption_summary: Drunkenness is treated purely as a disease to be managed, with no room left for the repentance Joel calls for, or else all use of wine is condemned against the plain text of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors bracket this subject. The first is total abstinence taught as a biblical requirement, which cannot be squared with a Bible in which wine maketh glad the heart of man, in which the Lord Jesus made a great quantity of it at a wedding and gave the cup at the supper, and in which Paul told Timothy to use a little for his stomach's sake. The dictionary holds Christian liberty here, with the warning Paul attaches to it about the weaker brother. The second error is the modern reflex that assigns drunkenness entirely to pathology, leaving the sufferer a patient and never a sinner — which removes the only door Joel offers, which is to turn to God with all the heart.

Scripture's own handling is neither. It names drunkenness as sin, lists it among the works of the flesh, and bars the drunkard from the kingdom in the same sentence as the covetous and the extortioner — and in the very next line tells the Corinthians that such were some of you, but ye are washed. It also recognises bondage: the drinkers of Joel 1 are asleep and have to be woken. The pastoral answer holds both, as the Reformed tradition has: real responsibility, real bondage, and a real deliverance that begins with the summons to awake and weep, and ends with the promise to restore the years the locust hath eaten.

etymology: From the Latin re- and commendare, to commit or entrust. Both uses describe a church sending men out by committing them to the grace of God, which is the New Testament's doctrine of commissioning in one phrase.
biblical_def: Luke closes the first missionary journey by naming where it began: “And thence sailed to Antioch, from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled” (Acts 14:26). The church at Antioch had not hired them or licensed them; it had committed them to the grace of God, and Luke marks the work as fulfilled by the same grace they were committed to. The second journey begins the same way after a sharp disagreement: “And Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God” (Acts 15:40). The original sending is recorded with its fasting and its laying on of hands: “And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away” (Acts 13:3). And Paul uses a kindred verb in his farewell to the Ephesian elders, committing them to the keeping he had been committed to: “And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified” (Acts 20:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines recommend as to commend to another's favorable notice, and to commit with prayers to the care of another.
webster_full: RECOMMEND, v.t. To praise to another; to offer or commend to another's notice, confidence or kindness.
RECOMMEND, v.t. To commit with prayers; to commend to the care and protection of another.
COMMEND, v.t. To commit; to entrust or give in charge; to deliver up to another with confidence.
ORDAIN, v.t. To set apart for an office; to appoint; to invest with ministerial functions.
MISSIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; one sent upon a mission.
scriptures: Acts 14:26
And thence sailed to Antioch, from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled.
Acts 15:40
And Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God.
Acts 13:3
And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
Acts 20:32
And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.
corruption_summary: Sending is reconceived as an institutional and professional transaction, so that a church's act of committing men to the grace of God becomes a matter of credentials, funding and organisational approval.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what a sending church actually does. Antioch fasted, prayed, laid hands on two men, and committed them to the grace of God — and that commitment is what Luke names when he describes their return. Boards, funding, training and accountability all have their place, and the New Testament assumes real oversight, since Paul and Barnabas reported back to the church that sent them. But the act itself is an entrusting to God's grace, and where that is replaced by an entrusting to structures the word has lost its meaning.

Acts 15:40 also deserves to be read with its context intact, because it is a healthier text than it is usually allowed to be. Paul and Barnabas had just parted over John Mark in a contention so sharp that they separated; the brethren then recommended Paul and Silas to the grace of God, and Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus. Luke reports the failure without comment and records that both missions went forward. Years later Paul asks for Mark, saying he is profitable to him for the ministry. The grace they were committed to proved larger than the quarrel that divided them.

pos: v. (agreed; joined in affirming what another had charged)
etymology: From the Latin assentire, to agree. It occurs once, of the crowd at Paul's trial before Felix adding their voices to the orator's accusation.
biblical_def: The orator Tertullus has just laid out a case against Paul before the governor, and the chorus follows: “And the Jews also assented, saying that these things were so” (Acts 24:9). Nobody adds evidence; they add agreement, which in a court is a different thing. Paul's answer exposes the gap: “Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me” (Acts 24:13). He then states plainly what is true, including the part they call heresy: “But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets” (Acts 24:14). The law itself had forbidden precisely the behaviour of the assenting crowd: “Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment” (Exodus 23:2). Agreement is not evidence, and a number of voices saying that these things were so does not make them so.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines assent as the act of the mind in admitting the truth of a proposition; and to assent as to admit as true, to agree.
webster_full: ASSENT, n. The act of the mind in admitting or agreeing to the truth of a proposition.
ASSENT, v.i. To admit as true; to agree, yield or concede; to express an agreement of the mind.
ACCUSATION, n. The act of charging with a crime or offense; the charge of an offense or crime.
ORATOR, n. A public speaker; an advocate employed to plead a cause.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
scriptures: Acts 24:9
And the Jews also assented, saying that these things were so.
Acts 24:13
Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me.
Acts 24:14
But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets:
Exodus 23:2
Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment:
corruption_summary: Consensus is treated as a form of evidence, so that the number of people affirming a claim is mistaken for the grounds of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke's sentence is a study in how accusation works. A hired orator frames the charge in flattering legal language, and the party assents, saying that these things were so. Their agreement adds volume and nothing else, and Paul's reply goes straight to the missing element: neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me. The law had anticipated this exact failure and forbidden it — thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil, neither speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment. Scripture's standard is two or three witnesses to a fact, not a majority to an impression.

The application to doctrine is direct and is one of the Reformation's permanent contributions. Rome's argument at Worms was substantially an argument from assent: the number of the fathers, the antiquity of the practice, the agreement of the church. Luther's answer was that unless he were convinced by Scripture and plain reason his conscience was captive to the word of God. That is sola Scriptura stated at a trial, and it is the same principle Paul used before Felix: what the many affirm must still be proved, and what is written in the law and in the prophets is what settles it.
roots_summary: Greek suntithemai (G4934), to agree together; kategoreo (G2723), to accuse; hairesis (G139), a sect or heresy; Hebrew rabbim (H7227), the many.
roots_lines: Greek suntithemai (G4934) — to place together, agree, assent; Acts 24:9.
Greek kategoreo (G2723) — to accuse, bring a charge; the accusers before Felix.
Greek hairesis (G139) — a sect or heresy; the way which they call heresy.
Hebrew rabbim (H7227) — the many, a multitude; Exodus 23:2.
Hebrew natah (H5186) — to turn aside, wrest; to wrest judgment after many.
usage: “And the Jews also assented, saying that these things were so” — agreement without evidence.
“Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me” — Paul's answer.
“Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil” — the statute behind it.

etymology: From answer, in the older sense of corresponding to. In Exodus it is a builder's word: the hanging at the gate of the court was made answerable to the hangings of the court — matched in measure to what stood beside it.
biblical_def: The word appears once, in the inventory of the tabernacle's courtyard: “And the hanging for the gate of the court was needlework, of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen: and twenty cubits was the length, and the height in the breadth was five cubits, answerable to the hangings of the court” (Exodus 38:18). The gate-screen was more richly worked than the plain hangings around it, and it was made to the same height, so that the entrance was beautiful without being irregular. Every measure in the structure was given beforehand: “According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it” (Exodus 25:9). The record closes by certifying compliance: “And Moses did look upon all the work, and, behold, they had done it as the LORD had commanded, even so had they done it: and Moses blessed them” (Exodus 39:43). The writer to the Hebrews explains why the measurements mattered: “Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount” (Hebrews 8:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines answerable as correspondent; agreeing with; suitable; proportionate.
webster_full: ANSWERABLE, a. Correspondent; agreeing with; in conformity with; suitable.
ANSWERABLE, a. Equal; correspondent; proportionate; as, the length was answerable to the breadth.
HANGING, n. Drapery hung or fastened to walls; the curtains of the tabernacle court.
PATTERN, n. An original or model proposed for imitation; the archetype; an exemplar.
NEEDLEWORK, n. Work executed with a needle; embroidery.
scriptures: Exodus 38:18

And the hanging for the gate of the court was needlework , of blue, and purple, and scarlet , and fine twined linen: and twenty cubits was the length, and the height in the breadth was five cubits, answerable to the hangings of the court.
Exodus 25:9
According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it.
Exodus 39:43
And Moses did look upon all the work, and, behold, they had done it as the LORD had commanded, even so had they done it: and Moses blessed them.
Hebrews 8:5

Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.
corruption_summary: The regulative principle is set aside in favour of whatever seems effective, and the tabernacle's insistence that everything be made answerable to a given pattern is treated as an Old Testament peculiarity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God specified His own worship and then checked the work. Moses did look upon all the work, and behold, they had done it as the LORD had commanded. Nothing in the tabernacle was left to the craftsman's preference — not the metals, not the measurements, not the colours of a gate-screen, not the height it had to match. The point is not that God is fastidious but that the structure was a shadow of heavenly things, and a shadow that departs from its object teaches a falsehood.

From this the Reformed churches derived the regulative principle of worship: what God has commanded in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. The principle is widely abandoned now in favour of a normative one — whatever is not forbidden may be introduced — and the practical result is that the question asked of a service is whether it works rather than whether it is commanded. Exodus does not ask whether a more striking gate-hanging would have drawn more worshippers. It records the measurements, and it records a man inspecting the work against them, and then blessing those who had made it answerable.

etymology: From advise, Old French aviser, to consider. The word occurs once, of the Philistine lords deliberating over whether to let David fight beside them — a council of pagans whose decision God used to keep His anointed clean.
biblical_def: The Chronicler reports how David came to be free of an impossible battle: “And there fell some of Manasseh to David, when he came with the Philistines against Saul to battle: but they helped them not: for the lords of the Philistines upon advisement sent him away, saying, He will fall to his master Saul to the jeopardy of our heads” (1 Chronicles 12:19). David had put himself in an intolerable position, marching with Achish against Israel, and the deliverance came not from his own wisdom but from his enemies' suspicion. The Philistine princes were blunt about it: “Wherefore now return, and go in peace, that thou displease not the lords of the Philistines” (1 Samuel 29:7). David's own reply is one of the more uncomfortable verses about him: “And David said unto Achish, But what have I done? and what hast thou found in thy servant so long as I have been with thee unto this day, that I may not go fight against the enemies of my lord the king?” (1 Samuel 29:8). He protests his willingness to go. Solomon states the doctrine the episode illustrates: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Proverbs 16:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines advisement as counsel; information; deliberation; consultation before determining.
webster_full: ADVISEMENT, n. Counsel; information; circumspection; deliberation; consultation.
ADVISE, v.t. To give counsel to; to offer an opinion, as worthy or expedient to be followed.
DELIBERATE, v.i. To weigh in the mind; to consider the reasons for and against a measure.
JEOPARDY, n. Exposure to death, loss or injury; hazard; danger; peril.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 12:19

And there fell some of Manasseh to David, when he came with the Philistines against Saul to battle: but they helped them not: for the lords of the Philistines upon advisement sent him away, saying, He will fall to his master Saul to the jeopardy of our heads.
1 Samuel 29:7
Wherefore now return, and go in peace, that thou displease not the lords of the Philistines.
1 Samuel 29:8

And David said unto Achish, But what have I done? and what hast thou found in thy servant so long as I have been with thee unto this day, that I may not go fight against the enemies of my lord the king?
Proverbs 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
corruption_summary: Providence is flattened into a promise that God will keep believers from the consequences of their choices, when Scripture here shows Him rescuing a man from a corner the man had talked himself into.
corruption_paragraphs: The episode is awkward for a sanitised David and is therefore rarely preached. He had fled to Gath, lived sixteen months under a Philistine king, raided and lied about it, and finally marched out with the enemy army against his own nation. Nothing in the account suggests God approved any of it. The rescue came through the distrust of pagan generals taking advisement about their own security, and David's recorded response was to ask why he could not go and fight. Scripture is not embarrassed to show its heroes being saved from themselves.

The doctrine this yields is more robust than the sentimental version. Providence is not a guarantee that a believer's foolishness will be painless; the same chapter has David return to find Ziklag burned and his wives taken, and his own men speaking of stoning him. What it does mean is that God governs the deliberations of men who neither know nor serve Him, and bends them to His purpose for His people. The lords of the Philistines took counsel about the jeopardy of their heads and thereby kept the LORD's anointed from lifting a sword against Israel on the day Saul fell. A man's heart deviseth his way; the LORD directeth his steps.
